items.q: Churros
items.pitch: Fried choux-style dough and cinnamon sugar from Spain and Latin America; the dipping chocolate seals it.

items.q: Crêpe Suzette
items.pitch: Thierry's pick. The crêpe batter is easy, but the orange butter and the flambé make it Suzette; the legend says a waiter set it alight by accident for the future Edward VII.

items.q: Kibbeh
items.pitch: Often called Lebanon's national dish: lamb, onion, pine nuts and seven spices could be kafta until the fine bulgur appears.

items.q: Tartiflette
items.pitch: Potatoes, lardons, onions and white wine from the Savoie ski slopes; it only took off in the 1980s, when the makers of the cheese pushed it.

items.q: Bibimbap
items.pitch: Korea's 'mixed rice' bowl: rice, spinach, beansprouts, carrots, beef and a fried egg, and the red chilli paste gives it away.

items.q: Tacos al pastor
items.pitch: Lebanese immigrants brought shawarma to Mexico and it became this: chilli-marinated pork carved off a spit. The pineapple tells you it's al pastor.

items.q: Knafeh
items.pitch: The Levantine cheese pastry: semolina or kataifi, butter, orange-blossom syrup and pistachios, and the melting white cheese makes it unmistakable.

items.q: Peking duck
items.pitch: Cucumber, spring onion and hoisin mean one thing to anyone who's had a Chinese takeaway in London or Paris.

items.q: Biryani
items.pitch: Saffron, crispy fried onions, yoghurt-marinated lamb and whole spices, layered and steamed; the rice reveals it.

items.q: Cassoulet
items.pitch: White beans, pork belly and Toulouse sausage, slow-baked; Castelnaudary, Carcassonne and Toulouse all claim it. The duck clinches it.

items.q: Vitello tonnato
items.pitch: Piedmont's cold sliced veal under a creamy sauce. Capers, anchovies and mayonnaise come first, then the twist that surprises everyone.

items.q: Mole poblano
items.pitch: Three kinds of dried chilli, sesame, almonds, raisins and cinnamon, and then a sweet surprise in Puebla's famous sauce.

items.q: Beef rendang
items.pitch: Beef slow-cooked dry in coconut milk with lemongrass, galangal and chilli; it topped CNN's 2011 readers' poll of the world's best foods.

items.q: Shish barak
items.pitch: Tiny Lebanese lamb dumplings cooked in hot yoghurt sauce with garlic and coriander; the Lebanese get it, everyone else learns it.

items.q: Feijoada
items.pitch: Brazil's national dish: smoked sausage, pork ribs, bacon and bay, served with orange slices and farofa.

items.q: Haggis
items.pitch: A gross-out reveal: sheep's heart, liver and lungs, oatmeal, suet and spices. Burns Night on 25 January in one bite.

items.q: Paris-Brest
items.pitch: A ring of choux pastry with flaked almonds, made around 1910 for the Paris–Brest–Paris bike race and shaped like a wheel.

items.q: Gin and Tonic

items.q: Kir Royale

items.q: Pimm's Cup

items.pitch: 26 sovereign states: France, Belgium, Switzerland, Luxembourg, Monaco, Canada, Haiti, a big block of West and Central Africa, Madagascar, Comoros, Seychelles, Djibouti, Rwanda, Burundi, Vanuatu. Twist for the room: Lebanon is NOT one (Arabic is its only official language). Data: Wikipedia list of de jure official languages.

items.q: Every country that borders Russia
items.pitch: A ring of 14 around a blank Russia: Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland (both via Kaliningrad), Belarus, Ukraine, Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, China, Mongolia, North Korea. Data: internationally recognised land borders.

items.q: Every country with more than 100 million people
items.pitch: The 16 giants: India, China, USA, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Brazil, Bangladesh, Russia, Mexico, Ethiopia, Japan, Philippines, Egypt, DR Congo and Vietnam (the newest, from 2023). Next: Iran (~91m), Turkey (~87m). Data: UN World Population Prospects 2024; Japan is shrinking but is still about 124m.

items.q: Every member of the Arab League
items.pitch: 22 members, from Mauritania to Oman, including the surprises Comoros, Djibouti and Somalia; Lebanon was a 1945 founder, and Syria was readmitted in 2023. Data: current membership list.

items.q: Every country whose national anthem has no words
items.pitch: Only three: Spain (the Marcha Real, so players stand silent), Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo. San Marino was the fourth until it adopted official lyrics in September 2025. Data: national anthems with no official lyrics.

items.q: Countries that lost a World Cup final and never won one
items.pitch: The heartbreak map, a companion to the winners map: the Netherlands (lost 1974, 1978, 2010), Hungary (1938, 1954), Czechoslovakia (1934, 1962; shade Czechia and Slovakia), Sweden (1958) and Croatia (2018). Stable until the 2030 World Cup. Data: every World Cup final, 1930 to 2026.

items.q: Every country with 'Guinea' in its name
items.pitch: Three in West Africa (Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Equatorial Guinea) and one on the other side of the world, Papua New Guinea, named by a 16th-century Spanish explorer who thought its people looked like those of the Guinea coast. Data: country names, stable.

items.q: Eiffel Tower
items.why: The most recognisable building on earth and everyone knows it is in Paris; the leg is won on whether you can find Paris on a borders-only map, so most pins land within 50 to 150 km.

items.q: Statue of Liberty
items.why: Instantly known and the city is obvious; the only skill is putting New York on the right stretch of the US east coast.

items.q: Colosseum
items.why: World-famous, city obvious. Rome sits halfway down the west side of the boot, which most people can hit.

items.q: Sydney Opera House
items.why: Everyone knows it; the test is the south-east corner of Australia. Pins placed 'somewhere in Australia' lose by 2,000 km, so it still separates the teams.

items.q: Taj Mahal
items.why: Universally known and most people know it is near Delhi; a pin on Delhi is only about 180 km out.

items.q: Great Pyramid of Giza
items.why: The city is obvious and Cairo sits right at the bottom of the Nile delta, an easy shape to find on a borders-only map.

items.q: Big Ben (Elizabeth Tower)
items.why: A home banker for the British guests and known to everyone else; the only question is how close to the Thames estuary the pin lands.

items.q: Machu Picchu
items.why: Everyone knows it is in Peru, but it is in the Andes 500 km south-east of Lima, not on the coast; pins on Lima lose.

items.q: Petra (Al-Khazneh, the Treasury)
items.why: Famous and the country is known, but Petra is in the south of Jordan, about 190 km south of Amman; the room's Middle East experts will beat a pin on Amman.

items.q: Angkor Wat
items.why: Many people know it, fewer can say 'Cambodia' straight away, and fewer still can find north-west Cambodia on the map. It rewards real knowledge but stays fair.

items.q: Neuschwanstein Castle
items.why: The 'Disney castle' is famous, but it sits right on the Austrian border in the Alps; a pin on Munich is about 90 km out, a pin in the middle of Germany 400 km or more.

items.q: Temple of Bacchus, Baalbek
items.why: Easy for the Lebanese guests, a real test for everyone else: Baalbek is in the Bekaa, about 65 km east-north-east of Beirut, near the Syrian border. Lebanon is tiny, so the pin has to be precise.

items.q: Alhambra
items.why: Well known, but people must remember 'Granada' and then place it in Andalusia, inland from the Costa del Sol. Pins on Seville or Madrid are 210 to 360 km out.

items.q: Iguazu Falls
items.why: Famous falls whose location people roughly know (where Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay meet) but rarely precisely. The falls are 2.7 km wide, so the point is the Wikidata centre.

items.q: Jeita Grotto
items.why: Show the name on the TV with this one: a cave photo alone is too ambiguous to be fair. Then it is pure placing: you must know Lebanon's famous grotto and put it in the hills just inland from Jounieh, about 15 km north-east of central Beirut. Teams who know it land within a few km; teams who don't can be a continent away. A great one for the Lebanese guests to show off.

items.q: Moai of Ahu Tongariki
items.why: Everyone recognises the Moai, almost nobody can place a speck of land in the Pacific 3,500 km west of Chile. Distances will be large for both teams, which makes it a fun one.

items.q: Chichén Itzá (El Castillo)
items.why: People know 'Mexico', but it is on the Yucatán peninsula, about 1,100 km east of Mexico City and 190 km west of Cancún; a pin on Mexico City is 1,100 km out.

items.q: Mont-Saint-Michel
items.why: The French guests know it; the hard part is the exact spot on the Normandy/Brittany border in the bay. Note the photo's own title wrongly says Brittany: it is in Normandy, by a few km.

items.q: Matterhorn
items.why: Recognisable (the Toblerone mountain) but people put it in the middle of Switzerland; it is on the Italian border in the far south of Valais, about 110 km south of Bern.

items.q: Victoria Falls
items.why: Known name, vague location: on the Zambezi between Zambia and Zimbabwe, about 950 km north of Johannesburg. Most pins land in the wrong country of southern Africa.

items.q: Beirut–Rafic Hariri International Airport
items.clues: Arabic and English side by side, and seven of the eight flights are ME, Middle East Airlines, whose home is Beirut (EY is Etihad). The destinations are MEA's network (Paris, London, Rome, Frankfurt, Dubai, Istanbul, Athens) and Beirut is the one city missing. Every flight number and time is real: it is the airport's own departure list for 22 October 2026.
items.why: Easy: the language plus the home airline give it away, and half the room is Lebanese.

items.q: Adolfo Suárez Madrid–Barajas Airport
items.clues: A Spanish board where most flights are IB, Iberia, Spain's flag carrier. Barcelona is on the board, so it is not Barcelona; the long-haul flights to Bogotá and New York point to Iberia's hub. Madrid is missing.
items.why: Easy: Spanish plus Iberia plus 'Barcelona is listed' leaves only Madrid.

items.q: Lisbon Airport (Humberto Delgado)
items.clues: Portuguese words (Embarque, Última chamada, Atrasado) and TP, TAP Air Portugal, on almost every flight. Porto and Funchal are on the board, so it is Portugal's other big airport; Luanda and São Paulo are TAP's Lusophone long-haul routes from its hub.
items.why: Easy: the language and the flag carrier point to Portugal, and with Porto listed it can only be Lisbon. (Blank status = on time, as on real boards.)

items.q: Athens International Airport
items.clues: The Greek alphabet and A3, Aegean Airlines, on seven of the eight flights. Thessaloniki and Heraklion are on the board, so it is not those; Aegean's hub is Athens, the city missing.
items.why: Easy: an alphabet nobody can mistake, plus the national airline.

items.q: Istanbul Airport
items.clues: Turkish words (Zamanında = on time, Gecikmeli = delayed, İptal = cancelled) and TK, Turkish Airlines, on almost every flight. Ankara, İzmir and Antalya are listed, so it is the one big Turkish city missing: Istanbul, TK's hub.
items.why: Easy at city level (Istanbul). The exact airport is IST; the trickier Sabiha Gökçen board is a hard leg.

items.q: Amsterdam Airport Schiphol
items.clues: Dutch words (Vertrek, Op tijd, Vertraagd, Geannuleerd) and KL, KLM, on most flights, plus HV (Transavia's Dutch arm). Curaçao is a Dutch Caribbean island, a classic KLM route from its only hub.
items.why: Easy: Dutch plus KLM can only be Amsterdam. (Real Schiphol screens are in English; the app draws this one in Dutch on purpose.)

items.q: Dubai International Airport
items.clues: Arabic and English, and the airline is EK, Emirates, on seven flights (FZ is flydubai). Emirates has a single hub, Dubai, and the destinations span every continent, as a giant hub's would.
items.why: Easy: Emirates is one of the best-known airlines in the world and it has one hub.

items.q: Frankfurt Airport
items.clues: German words (Abflug, Pünktlich, Verspätet, Annulliert) and German city names (Rom, München, Laibach = Ljubljana), so a German-speaking airport. LH, Lufthansa, has two hubs, Frankfurt and Munich, and München is on the board, so it must be Frankfurt. DE is Condor, also based in Frankfurt.
items.why: Medium: the language narrows it to Germany, Austria or Switzerland; you need 'Lufthansa hub' plus 'Munich is listed' to finish.

items.q: Munich Airport
items.clues: German board, Lufthansa everywhere, so one of its two hubs. Frankfurt is on the board, so this is the other one: Munich. Hamburg, Berlin and Köln are listed too, which rules them out.
items.why: Medium: the mirror image of the Frankfurt leg (deal one to each team). You must notice which hub is missing.

items.q: Zurich Airport
items.clues: German again, but the airline is LX, Swiss (and WK, Edelweiss), not Lufthansa, so Switzerland. Genf (Geneva) is on the board, which leaves Swiss's hub, Zurich.
items.why: Medium: you have to know that LX is Swiss and that German is not only spoken in Germany.

items.q: Brussels Airport
items.clues: Every word in French AND Dutch, which only Belgium does. SN is Brussels Airlines, and Kinshasa is its trademark route to the former Belgian Congo.
items.why: Medium: the bilingual board is a lovely clue, but people need to connect French plus Dutch to Belgium.

items.q: Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport
items.clues: French, Air France on seven flights, Nice and Toulouse on the board, so the capital. Since Air France left Orly in 2026 (it keeps only Corsica flights there), any Air France flight to Nice, Toulouse or long-haul is from Charles de Gaulle.
items.why: Medium: 'Paris' is easy; naming Charles de Gaulle needs the long-haul Air France clue. Give the leg for 'Paris'; the Orly board is the hard twin where the exact airport is required.

items.q: Singapore Changi Airport
items.clues: English gives nothing away, but SQ (Singapore Airlines) and TR (Scoot, its low-cost arm) fly every route. Destinations fan out across Asia and Australia, with London and New York.
items.why: Medium: an English board saved by the home airline code. Teams who know SQ win.

items.q: Geneva Airport
items.clues: French, but Paris is ON the board (Orly), so this is not Paris. LX (Swiss) flies to Zurich and New York, so a Swiss airport, and a French-speaking one: Geneva. Lots of easyJet (U2) too: its Swiss arm, easyJet Switzerland (code DS), is based in Geneva.
items.why: Medium: the French language is a red herring until you spot Paris on the board and the Swiss airline.

items.q: Paris Orly Airport
items.clues: French and Paris is missing, so a Paris airport, but which? No Air France long-haul: Air France appears only to Corsica (it left Orly in 2026 except Corsican public-service routes). Instead Transavia (TO), Vueling, Air Algérie, and leisure long-haul carriers to the overseas departments (Air Caraïbes TX, French Bee BF): that is Orly.
items.why: Hard: the language and city are easy, the second-airport question is not. Only the exact airport counts.

items.q: London Gatwick Airport
items.clues: English, a flight to Edinburgh (so a UK airport that is not Edinburgh) and London missing. Mostly easyJet (U2) and low-cost carriers, plus BA flying to the Caribbean (Antigua) and to sun spots: that is Gatwick, not Heathrow (no Virgin, no Qantas, no long list of flag carriers).
items.why: Hard: an English board with no home-airline giveaway, and a city with six airports.

items.q: London Heathrow Airport
items.clues: English, Edinburgh on the board, London missing. No easyJet or Ryanair, but BA long-haul, Virgin Atlantic, United, Air India, Cathay, Qantas and MEA: most of the world's flag carriers fly to Heathrow, not Gatwick.
items.why: Hard: same language and city as Gatwick; you must read the airline mix.

items.q: John F. Kennedy International Airport
items.clues: English, US domestic flights (Boston, Atlanta, Los Angeles) plus a big international list: a US gateway with no single home airline. New York is missing; it is JFK, not Newark, because there is no United (UA), Newark's hub airline, and Emirates' New York to Milan flight goes from JFK.
items.why: Hard: English board, three home-ish airlines (Delta, JetBlue, American), and a city with two big airports.

items.q: Tokyo Haneda Airport

board.dest: ニューヨーク New York-JFK

items.clues: Japanese, JAL (JL) and ANA (NH), Tokyo missing, so a Tokyo airport. Haneda, not Narita: Skymark (BC) and the Kobe flight are Haneda-only among Tokyo's airports, JAL's London and New York flights and Delta's Atlanta flight leave from Haneda, and a board this full of JAL/ANA domestic routes (Sapporo, Fukuoka, Okinawa) is Haneda's; Narita's domestic flights are mostly low-cost carriers.
items.why: Hard: the language gives Japan and the airlines give Tokyo, but Haneda versus Narita needs real knowledge.

items.q: Istanbul Sabiha Gökçen International Airport
items.clues: Turkish words, Ankara/İzmir/Antalya on the board, Istanbul missing. But no Turkish Airlines: it is Pegasus (PC) and AJet (VF), the low-cost carriers, flying to London-Stansted rather than Heathrow. That is Istanbul's Asian-side airport, Sabiha Gökçen.
items.why: Hard: looks just like the easy Istanbul board; only the airline codes say it is the city's second airport.
